capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user

inputs.source: User's direct prompt in the desktop client
Issue text in the user's public GitHub repository, authorable by any GitHub user

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: 'The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private.'
instructions.note: The stated task ('look at open issues in my public repo') needs no private-repo access, but the credential granted to the agent covers every repository the user owns. The capability exceeds the task's implied authority.

elements.name: GHCR image registry / github-mcp-server upstream maintainers

controls.name: Per-tool-call human approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the client outside the model, but arguments are collapsed by default so the approver typically reviews a summary, not the raw destination and payload. High call volume per session (approval fatigue) and a more persuasive model (model_upgrade) both erode effectiveness; see control_decay.md's approval-fatigue scoring.

controls.name: Containerized MCP server execution (docker run --rm)
controls.decay_rationale: Isolates the MCP server process from the host filesystem, but does not constrain what the GitHub API token itself can read or write. The exfiltration path runs through the token/API, not host access, so this control does not cover either sink.

controls.name: Repository-scoped least-privilege credential
controls.decay_rationale: A token (or GitHub App installation) scoped only to the public repository would make private-repo data unreachable from this agent under any model behavior, severing the path.

controls.name: Raw-action approval review (expanded arguments by default)
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the full destination repository and diff before approval, rather than a collapsed summary, would make the gate independent of model persuasiveness.

controls.name: Digest-pinned / signed MCP server image
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server to a verified digest would prevent a silent swap of the tool definitions on a later docker run, closing the supply-chain vector of this finding.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue content drives private-repo read into a public pull request

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user opens an issue in the public repo containing instructions aimed at the agent.
Agent follows the injected instructions and reads confidential content from a private repository using the broad, repo-wide PAT.

Agent opens a pull request on the public repository embedding the private content, exposing it to the world (egress). The sink's effective data sensitivity is confidential, inherited from the earlier read, per the path-sensitivity rule.

findings.residual_rationale: Rubric credits (step 2, approval gate on an S3 sink, model_summary review) compute a floor of moderate (critical minus two tiers). Residual is rated high instead because the runtime notes describe real approval-fatigue conditions the classification cannot express numerically: users approve many calls per session with arguments collapsed by default, which is the documented failure mode behind the public GitHub MCP disclosure this case backtests.

forecast.watch_signal: Client changes 'approve each call' to 'always allow for this tool/session'; autonomy level raised from A1/A2; or the underlying model is upgraded to one that writes more persuasive or selectively incomplete call summaries.

evidence.observation: The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so cap.read_private_repo and cap.create_pr_public share the same broad credential.
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making in.public_issue an untrusted (U) source reachable by any outsider.
The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, matching the model_summary approval-fatigue pattern.
A single GitHub MCP server is configured with one PAT passed via environment variable, shared across all repo-scoped tool calls.

recommendations.action: Scope the credential (fine-grained PAT or GitHub App installation token) to only the public repository this agent is meant to browse; remove private-repo access entirely for this agent.
Default the approval UI to raw-action review: show the full destination repository, diff, and arguments before approving create_pull_request or private-repo reads, rather than a collapsed summary.
Log and alert when a pull request created on a public repository contains content read from a private repository in the same session.
Treat issue and comment text as untrusted data; run an injection-detection pass before letting issue content drive privileged tool calls.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server image enables a tool-definition rug pull (ASI04)

attack_path.note: The docker image reference carries no digest or signature pin, so a compromised or malicious update to the upstream image is pulled automatically on the next `docker run`.
A rug-pulled tool definition can silently alter what get_file_contents does or reports, while keeping a benign-looking name and description.
The same altered server can exfiltrate private data into or through the public-repo write path, independent of any issue injection.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

findings.residual_rationale: The step-2 approval-gate credit computes a floor of moderate, but the same approval-fatigue condition documented in this design (collapsed arguments, high call volume) means a relabeled or obfuscated tool action is unlikely to be caught at approval time, so residual is rated high rather than the bare floor.

forecast.watch_signal: Image digest or version pulled by `docker run` changes without a corresponding reviewed config change; additional unpinned MCP servers added to mcpServers.json.

evidence.observation: The docker image reference 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' has no digest or version pin, so each `docker run` can silently pull an updated image.
The same collapsed-argument, per-call approval gate that governs ordinary use is also the only control standing between a rug-pulled tool definition and the private-repo-to-public-PR path.

recommendations.action: Pin ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server to a specific verified digest and verify signature before each pull, instead of a floating tag.
Monitor for changes to the pulled image digest or version and alert before the new image is used.

rating.rationale: Both findings are U-equivalent sources (an issue any outsider can author, and an unpinned upstream image any publisher can alter) reaching an S3 sink (confidential private-repo data flowing into a public, irreversible pull request through a broadly-scoped PAT), so inherent is critical with no caps applying (autonomy is A1, not A0, and no autonomy cap reduces it). The only material control is a per-call approval prompt that is structurally present but classified partially_dependent because arguments are collapsed by default (model_summary review). The rubric floor from that credit is moderate, but residual is held at high because the design explicitly describes high call volume and collapsed-argument approval, the same approval-fatigue condition documented for this case in control_decay.md. Forecast returns to critical because model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or control_removal each defeat the only control covering the path, restoring the uncontrolled inherent tier. The single control whose decay drives the forecast is ctl.tool_call_prompt.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration (the provided mcp.json and runtime notes) at the time of review, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt was provided; instruction-level issues are inferred from the runtime notes and capability list only, which lowers confidence on anything beyond the unbounded_scope finding.

No full tool manifest for the github-mcp-server was provided beyond the two named tools; other tools the server exposes (for example issue comments or repo administration) are not assessed and could open additional egress paths.
